result:
Neither 6 nor 7 holds up, because there are counterexamples with no Berge-C₅³ for n = 6, 7 and 8. Solution 2 is also wrong, since it ends at 3, which is impossible. My own check suggests n₀ is at least 9, though I haven't determined it exactly.

**Why a 4-edge blocks C₅³.** If a 5-set contains a 4-edge Q, every cyclic order of the 5-set has Q as four consecutive vertices. So one window of four consecutive vertices is Q, and the two consecutive triples in that window must both be covered by Q. If Q is a block whose triples no other edge covers, they cannot get distinct edges, so no Berge-C₅³ lies on that 5-set.

**n = 6.** Take the blocks 1234, 1256 and 3456, and cover the remaining triples with 3-edges. Each of the six 5-subsets contains one block, so there is no Berge-C₅³. Hence n₀ > 6.

**n = 7.** Take the complements of the seven Fano lines as 4-edges. They pairwise meet in 2 points, so no triple lies in two of them. A 5-set is the complement of a pair, and every pair lies in exactly one line, so every 5-set contains exactly one block. Cover the other triples with 3-edges. There is again no Berge-C₅³, so n₀ > 7.

**n = 8.** The Steiner system S(3,4,8) has 14 blocks, each lying in four 5-sets, which gives 56 incidences. There are 56 five-sets in total, so each contains exactly one block. This is another counterexample, so n₀ > 8.

Solution 1's answer of 7 is therefore false, and Solution 3's answer of 6 is false for the same reason. Solution 1 is still the closest of the three, since its answer is nearer the true value. Solution 2's answer of 3 is the furthest off.

CHOICE: 1
